I. INTRODUCTION AND EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Oncor Electric Delivery Company (“Oncor”) and LCRA Transmission Services
Corporation (“LCRA TSC”) (collectively the “Applicants”) filed a joint application
(“Application”) with the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) to amend their
certificates of convenience and necessity for the proposed Bell County East Switch to Big Hill
Substation 765-kV Transmission Line Project (“Project”) in Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell,
Lampasas, Llano, Mason, McCullouch, Menard, Milam, Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green,

and Williamson Counties in Docket No. 59475 (“Docket”).

 This is a long, expensive, and highly contested Project that the Administrative Law Judges
(“ALJs”) and the Commission must determine which route, either a route filed by the Applicants
or by an Intervenor through a Requests for Information (“RFI”) Route, and best satisfy the
requirements of Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) § 37.056(c)(4)(A)-() of the Texas
Utilities Code and 16 Texas Administrative Code (“TAC”) § 25.101. PURA § 37.056(c) states:

“(t]he Commission shall grant each certificate on a nondiscriminatory basis
after considering: (1) the adequacy of existing service; (2) the need for
additional service; (3) the effect of granting the certificate on the recipient
of the certificate and any electric utility serving the proximate area; and (4)
other factors, such as: (A) community values; (B) recreational and park
areas; (C) historical and aesthetic values; (D) environmental integrity; and

(E) the probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to consumers
in the area if the certificate is granted...”

The Commission’s rules in 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) elaborate on the statutory criteria,
stating an application for a new transmission line must address in PURA § 37.056(c) and in
considering those criteria, engineering constraints, and costs, the line must be routed to the
extent reasonable to moderate the impact on the affected community and landowners unless
grid reliability and security dictate otherwise. (Emphasis Added)

As anticipated, numerous Initial Briefs were filed by Intervenors in support of their
respective positions regarding what route(s) they approve of and what route(s) they oppose.
Interventors not affected by the Applicants’ “Best Meets” Route, Route 894, support the
Applicants’ positions. Similarly, landowners who are unaffected by the recommendation of Public
Utility Commission Staff (“Staff”), Route 487, support this route.

Link R1 Landowners further show support for Route 894 Western Mod. 1 as the route that
best satisfies the requirements of PURA and TAC. Furthermore, Link R1 Landowners also present
evidence as to why routes not using links “P2-R1” are advantageous. This Reply Brief responds
to the arguments and concerns voiced in the Post-Hearing Initial Briefs (“Initial Briefs”) of other

Intervenors in this Docket. Specifically, this Reply Brief responds to Link N12/P1 Intervenors

 (“N12/P1 Intervenors”) who advocate for routes that do not use Links N12 or P1, which includes
Route 894 Western Mod. | or similar forward progressing routes.

While trying to provide adequate support for their arguments, N12/P1 Intervenors
attempted to tun the Applicants’ data and routing of the factors into a “math equation” and failed
to look beyond the data/numbers into the holistic routing. Holistically, Route 894 Western Mod. 1
improves routing in the western quarter of the Project, along Route 894. Likewise, the use of the
western links advocated for in 894 Western Mod. 1 can and should be applied to any other route
to improve the western routing. In addition to basing arguments on the numbers, arguments made
in Initial Briefs that look to the non-quantitative facts fail for numerous reasons that are addressed

herein.

Il. ROUTING CRITERIA

Numerous topics of concern were identified by members of the affected communities
throughout the Study Area; these concerns were assembled from answers to questionnaires, open
meetings, and direct testimony of Intervenors. Topics of concern in this Project generally include
community values, recreational and park areas, aesthetics, historical and cultural values,
engineering constraints, paralleling, prudent avoidance, cost, and length. The Applicants seek a

recommendation of any filed route, or “along any forward-progressing route composed of filed

route links and determined to be constructible,”’ One of these forward-progressing routes is

Route 894 Western Mod. 1.? Holistically, routing across the western quarter of the Project can
greatly improve many of the routes. To compare what is at issue in the western quarter, one must
look at differences between the western links, which is done by comparing Route 894 and Route

894 Western Mod. 1, where the use of Links N12 and/or P1 are superior to Links N3, P2, and R1.

 All the above-mentioned links bisect rural land, which is predominantly used for ranching
and hunting. The ALJs and Commission must look at what distinguishes these western links from
each other by looking at the data and the qualitative, non-quantifiable facts such as aesthetics and
community values. Link N3 and Link P2 (Menard County), and Link R1 (Schleicher County) are
at the western edge of the Texas Hill Country, with undisturbed land and limited fragmentation by
existing transmission lines.* These areas are not fragmented by industrial infrastructure, such as
those used for solar and wind farms. While this is one of the first major distinctions between Links
“N3-P2-R1” and Links “N12-P1,” there are many other impacts that should be considered in the

final route determination.
